title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications produced by an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The preregistered estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task, reused across both arms); the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We executed N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) using the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier. All archived scoring artifacts report safe outcomes for every paired episode: baseline safe = 240/240, guarded safe = 240/240. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00 with 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract, the paired contrast can only arise if the single shared candidate fails validation or a validator‑triggered repair is applied; in this run every shared candidate passed deterministic validation and no repairs were invoked, producing a degenerate paired outcome. We present the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting and statistics, an evidence‑based failure analysis of why the primary contrast was uninformative, and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future GVR evaluations that will produce informative paired contrasts.

sections.introduction:
Translating operator intent into safe, executable network configuration is a central operational challenge. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic orchestration frameworks promise convenient intent translation, but text‑level fidelity metrics do not capture activity ordering, transient invariants, or protected‑resource constraints essential for safe application in live networks. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are executed in device emulators and deterministically scored—exposes semantic failure modes (ordering mistakes, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) that text‑only tests miss. A recurring architectural remedy is the generate–validate–repair (GVR) pattern: an LLM produces a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are detected. Prior work documents GVR‑style patterns across configuration repair and program‑repair domains and suggests they can reduce syntactic and many semantic errors, but open empirical questions remain about measurable verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and about how evaluation contracts affect paired causal contrasts.

This paper reports a preregistered, paired GVR experiment executed in an emulation‑grounded benchmark. The study asked a single, precisely defined question: Does integrating a deterministic verifier into a GVR pipeline reduce the paired unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline) relative to an LLM‑only pipeline under matched intent tasks, distribution shift, and adversarial prompts? The study used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task shared across arms) and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair in the guarded arm. We preserve and reference archived artifacts backing every principal numeric claim. Our contributions are: (1) an artifact‑grounded execution and analysis of the preregistered paired GVR test (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01); (2) an explicit mapping between the preregistered estimand and archived analysis outputs so reported numbers are verifiable; and (3) a failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.
sections.related_work: Executable NetOps benchmarks and emulation frameworks have been proposed to surface workflow and planning faults for LLM agents rather than only measuring textual fidelity; NetConfArena is an example of such a closed‑loop benchmark that emphasizes executable tests and hidden scoring. Work on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and demonstrates that deterministic validators often enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, but semantic coverage depends on verifier design and fault taxonomy. Surveys and recent position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising patterns for operational NetOps automation and safety. Engineering precedent from configuration analysis tools (e.g., Batfish) demonstrates the value of formalized invariants and incremental verification. Our study differs by (a) preregistering a single paired estimand; (b) executing under shared_initial_candidate semantics (explicitly constraining generator calls); (c) using emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring; and (d) archiving per‑call traces and validator traces to permit direct reconciliation of the measured estimand with stored artifacts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 denotes a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied; safe_apply = 0 denotes no such violation. The analysis executor and mapping from archived artifacts were preregistered: the paired contingency and condition summaries produced by the registered paired_binary_analysis executor map directly to the estimand, and the bootstrap parameters (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) are fixed in the archived analysis log.

Design and generation semantics: The design is paired with exactly N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks; each task was executed under both arms. Task composition was blocked as in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), and adversarial‑prompt 20% (48). A deterministic task generator produced task payloads including initial states, required sequences, and preserved‑field constraints. Crucially, execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: the adapter produced exactly one initial LLM generation per task, and both the baseline and guarded episodes used that same generation. Under this contract, paired differences can only arise if (i) the shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation or (ii) the guarded arm requests and applies a validator‑triggered repair that changes the final configuration relative to the baseline.

Model, verifier, and adapter contract: Execution declared gpt-5-mini as the model and used a deterministic network verifier in the guarded pipeline. The adapter permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task in the guarded condition. Model sampling metadata and provider call events were archived for audit. The preregistration specified a retry policy for infra failures (up to two automated retries) and predefined treatments for flagged items (exclusions for 'possible false‑safe' items in the primary analysis; planned sensitivity analyses if exclusions occurred).

Scoring and analysis: Final outcomes are binary (safe vs unsafe) determined by deterministic emulator execution and invariant checks recorded in validator traces. The primary analysis used an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs together with a paired bootstrap percentile CI for the difference (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Secondary planned outputs included median repair counts and model‑call budgets per task. The preregistration and analysis plan, including multiplicity handling, were fixed before observing outcomes.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed in accordance with the preregistered plan. Planned_episode_count = 480 and completed_episode_count = 480, yielding complete_pair_count = 240. The provider call audit recorded exactly one shared initial generation per task (hosted model call events = 240) and overall model_calls_used = 240 consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics. No infrastructure failures required post‑preregistration exclusion and no pairs were excluded from the primary analysis.

Primary binary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. The archived condition summary reports baseline successes = 240, baseline failures = 0 (baseline unsafe_apply = 0), and guarded successes = 240, guarded failures = 0 (guarded unsafe_apply = 0). The paired contingency is n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. The paired risk difference (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) and the exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All numbers above are traceable to archived analysis artifacts produced by the registered analysis executor.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied: repair_attempts = 0 across the archived repair logs. Representative validator traces show validation_before and validation_after snapshots, required_command_count fields, and explicit validator PASS results for every shared candidate. Because every shared candidate passed deterministic validation, the guarded arm did not need to alter any final configurations; as a result the baseline and guarded final configurations are identical for all tasks and subgroups (in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, adversarial). Planned sensitivity channels for 'possible false‑safe' items and infra failures were unused because no such flags occurred.

Subgroup slices: The subgroup breakdown (in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, adversarial) is degenerate: all subgroups have zero unsafe applies in both arms. Thus per‑subgroup paired contrasts are numerically identical to the global result (difference = 0.00).
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation of the null paired contrast: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics ensured exactly one initial LLM generation per task was shared across arms. Under the adapter contract, the guarded arm could only differ from baseline by invoking a validator‑triggered repair when the shared candidate failed validation. In this execution every shared candidate passed deterministic validation; no repairs were requested or applied. This mechanistic chain—shared initial candidate that always passes validation → zero repairs → identical final outcomes—fully explains the degenerate paired contingency and is supported by the archived provider call audit and validator traces.

Design tradeoffs and interpretability: Shared_initial_candidate semantics provides a tightly paired comparison on the same LLM sample and reduces model‑call budgets, but it also constrains the possible causal contrasts: if the generator rarely fails the verifier, the guarded pipeline cannot demonstrate benefit. Conversely, designs that allow independent initial generations per arm or that intentionally inject generator variability provide the verifier more opportunities to act, at the cost of requiring larger model‑call budgets and careful blocking to preserve comparability. Our empirical result therefore does not show that verifiers are unhelpful in general; it shows that under the specific, preregistered generation contract and test corpus the verifier had no opportunity to change any paired outcome because all shared candidates passed.

Recommendations for informative future GVR evaluations (artifact‑grounded): (1) To measure verifier causal effect, avoid shared_initial_candidate semantics or permit independent initial generations per arm so discordant generator outputs can occur; the archived provider call audit highlights the practical difference in model calls. (2) Increase the repair budget (allow multiple repair iterations) and record repair prompts/edits to study repair search dynamics. (3) Strengthen adversary protocols (beyond a single fixed seed) to generate adaptive prompt manipulations that are more likely to induce validator failures; the preregistered contamination controls show how adversarial tagging can be reproducibly incorporated. (4) Augment deterministic validators with cross‑checks against emulator outcomes and planned false‑safe detection logic to identify potential validator blind spots; archive flagged mismatches for sensitivity analyses. Implementing these changes will increase the probability of observing informative discordant pairs and thereby permit a nondegenerate paired estimator.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference of 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). This degenerate contrast arose because the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced exactly one shared LLM output per task and every shared output passed deterministic validation; therefore the guarded arm had no occasion to apply repairs and could not create discordant pairs. The archived artifacts supporting these claims include the preregistration, provider call audit, validator traces, and analysis artifacts. The principal methodological lesson is that generation semantics and adversary strength are decisive for whether a paired GVR test can detect verifier benefit. We provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future experiments designed to produce informative paired contrasts by varying generation semantics, repair budgets, and adversary power.

limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompting strategies, or prompt templates.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes observed verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier implements a finite set of semantic checks; uncovered fault classes may remain undetected and require expanded verifier rule sets or cross‑checks with emulator outcomes.
